I think the code is **RWMF**. I worked this out by reading the weights by hand without running anything, so it isn't checked by computation.

**Four hidden units do nothing.** Units 32 to 35 (the last four rows of W1) don't look like the rest of the network:

- Their W1 weights are all small (about ±0.05 to 0.19) and follow an alternating pattern. They look like filler rather than learned values.
- Their biases are very negative: −2.82, −2.87, −2.77 and −2.70. Every other bias in b1 lies between −0.45 and 0.65.
- In any position, each cell turns on exactly one of its three inputs. So the most these units can receive from the board is the sum of their largest weight per cell, roughly 1.5 at most. That is well short of what it takes to overcome a bias near −2.8.
- So these units always output zero. Whatever is in their columns of W2 never reaches the scores, and the network plays exactly as it would without them. That makes them a safe place to hide something.

**Where the code is.** These four biases are the only values written with two decimals instead of three. If you ignore the "−2." part, the two digits are ASCII codes:

| Unit | Bias | Number | ASCII letter |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32 | −2.82 | 82 | R |
| 33 | −2.87 | 87 | W |
| 34 | −2.77 | 77 | M |
| 35 | −2.70 | 70 | F |

The same four units' columns in W2 just alternate between positive and negative values with no clear message, so I read them as more filler.

CODE: RWMF
